== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / No information — Because the total number of interviewees, invited stakeholders, and observed meetings across 2001-2004 is never reported, study non-response or participant drop-out cannot be evaluated (though low attendance by marginalized residents at public participation forums is substantively noted on PDF Page 13, Section 6.5, p. 207).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Not applicable / Uncontrolled (qualitative comparative case narrative without causal identification) — Historical apartheid privilege, racial classification, income/time resources, literacy/numeracy, and geographic context differ simultaneously between the Ruensveld/Duivenhoks commercial farming areas and Kassiesbaai, though the author qualitatively notes competing explanations for non-participation such as household poverty priorities (jobs, housing, education) and potential trust in the ANC state (PDF Page 9 Footnote 11, p. 203; PDF Page 13 Section 6.5, p. 207).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate (descriptive statutory and institutional framing) — Accurately identifies the post-apartheid legal architecture governing water resources and services, including the National Water Act (Act 36 of 1998, Schedule 6(1)(l) and Chapter 2, Part 1, Section 5(3)), the Water Services Act (Act 108 of 1997), the 1996 Cabinet abolition of riparian water rights, historical Soil Conservation Act (No. 48 of 1946) networks, and Catchment Management Agency (CMA) / Water User Association (WUA) mandates across 19 Water Management Areas (PDF Pages 2-5, 8-10, pp. 196-199, 202-204), though legal rules are summarized narratively rather than systematically coded.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: High concern — No interview guide, observation protocol, audio-recording or transcription procedure, language/translation handling, or researcher reflexivity is reported, creating substantial risk of observer and social-desirability bias when assessing sensitive constructs such as shame, ignorance, and institutional distrust across sharp racial and technocratic divides.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak — Governance outcomes (trust, voice, agency, shame) and local water service conditions (poor water taste/scarcity in Kassiesbaai, lack of water at farm schools cited from a 1999 basin report, and commercial pipeline network metrics cited from secondary history) rely on isolated illustrative quotes and secondary anecdotes without standardized or systematic measurement across households or forums.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: High concern — With no Methods section, no inventory of interviews or observed meetings, and no transparent qualitative coding framework, brief illustrative excerpts from five interviews and three CMA meeting utterances (2001-2004) are selectively woven into theoretical commentary, leaving high risk of selective quotation and confirmation bias.
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern — The two Breede-Overberg case narratives (Ruensveld/Duivenhoks commercial farmers vs. Kassiesbaai fishing village) were purposively chosen to illustrate contrasting social networks (PDF Page 4, Section 4, p. 198), and the paper reports zero sampling frame, inclusion criteria, sample size, or recruitment strategy for interview respondents or observed CMA meetings.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was there a clear statement of the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: The Abstract and Introduction clearly formulate the paper's central objective: examining how unequal relations of knowledge and power in post-apartheid South African water governance restrict agency, inhibit trust-building, and perpetuate feelings of shame that obstruct participatory water policy reform under the National Water Act and Water Services Act.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 1 of 18], Abstract (p. 195); [PDF Pages 2-3 of 18], Sections 1.1-1.2 (pp. 196-197)

domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative approach combining stakeholder interviews, observation of Catchment Management Agency (CMA) public participation forums and informal corridor ('stoep') interactions, and comparative local case narratives is appropriate for investigating subjective experiences of shame, discursive exclusion, and interpersonal/institutional trust.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 3-4 of 18], Sections 2-4 (pp. 197-198); [PDF Pages 11-15 of 18], Sections 6.3-7.1 (pp. 205-209)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the research design appropriate to address the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: Although contrasting historically privileged commercial farming networks (Ruensveld/Duivenhoks) with a marginalized coloured fishing village (Kassiesbaai) inside the same Breede-Overberg Water Management Area is conceptually coherent, the paper lacks any Methods section explaining or justifying the overall research design, site selection criteria, or how 2001-2004 fieldwork studies were integrated with secondary historical materials.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Page 4 of 18], Section 4 (p. 198); [PDF Pages 15-16 of 18], Footnote 17 (pp. 209-210)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the recruitment strategy appropriate to the aims of the research?
domain_ratings.justification: No information is provided on how interviewees (an Overberg Water Board respondent, a Kassiesbaai councillor, an Overberg WMA consultant, a small-scale farmer, and another local councillor) or observed CMA meetings were identified, sampled, or recruited, nor whether any targeted stakeholders declined to participate.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 5, 7, 11, 13, 14, 15 of 18], Sections 4.1, 4.2, 6.3, 6.5, 7, 7.1 (pp. 199, 201, 205, 207, 208, 209) — absence of recruitment reporting

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data collected in a way that addressed the research issue?
domain_ratings.justification: Parenthetical attributions show primary interviews and CMA meeting observations in the Breede-Overberg WMA between September 2001 and February 2004, and Footnote 17 briefly mentions water and sanitation case studies conducted in June-August 2003 and January-May 2004, but there is no reporting of total sample size, interview format/guides, observation protocols, recording/transcription methods, language of interviews, or data saturation.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Has the relationship between researcher and participants been adequately considered?
domain_ratings.justification: Despite centering the analysis on racialized power asymmetries, expert vs. lay hierarchies, and feelings of embarrassment and shame among marginalized water users, the author provides zero reflexive discussion of her own background, institutional positionality, or how her presence in interviews, committee venues, and informal 'stoep' spaces shaped respondent disclosures.
domain_ratings.where_found: Full text ([PDF Pages 1-18 of 18], pp. 195-212; author bio on [PDF Page 18 of 18], p. 212 notes professional background only, with no methodological reflexivity in the study)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Have ethical issues been taken into consideration?
domain_ratings.justification: Respondents are cited anonymously by role, location, and month/year, which preserves basic anonymity, but the article reports nothing on informed consent procedures, permission to observe and quote public/informal 'stoep' discussions, or institutional ethics review.
domain_ratings.where_found: Full text ([PDF Pages 1-16 of 18], pp. 195-210) — absence of ethics reporting

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the data analysis sufficiently rigorous?
domain_ratings.justification: No qualitative coding, thematic analysis procedure, corpus scope, or triangulation protocol is described. Short excerpts from a handful of interviews, meeting utterances, and secondary texts (e.g., Wilson 1999; Breede River Basin Study 1999) are used illustratively to support pre-existing sociological and social-capital theories without systematic presentation of counter-evidence.
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 4-15 of 18], Sections 4-7.1 (pp. 198-209) — absence of analytic/coding methods

domain_ratings.domain_name: Is there a clear statement of findings?
domain_ratings.justification: The thematic findings are clearly stated and synthesized: apartheid-era state-farmer networks endowed white commercial agriculturists with technical literacy and institutional trust, whereas technocratic IWRM/CMA framing alienates previously excluded black and coloured water users and elected councillors, triggering silence, 'fobbing off' by officials, and feelings of shame. The author also briefly notes alternative explanations for non-participation (poverty priority rankings and potential trust in the ANC government).
domain_ratings.where_found: [PDF Pages 7-16 of 18], Sections 4.3, 5, 6, 7, and 8 (pp. 201-210); Footnote 11 ([PDF Page 9 of 18], p. 203)

domain_ratings.justification: The study offers valuable conceptual and policy insights into the 'legal last mile' of South Africa's National Water Act (Act 36 of 1998) and Water Services Act (Act 108 of 1997), highlighting how formal multi-stakeholder decentralization (CMAs and WUAs) can reproduce exclusion when technical discourse and shame silence marginalized representatives. However, its standalone empirical weight and transferability are substantially weakened by the complete absence of transparent fieldwork and analytic reporting.
domain_ratings.rating: Moderately valuable conceptual and contextual contribution to understanding participatory water governance bottlenecks in South Africa, but empirically limited by severe under-reporting of fieldwork and analytic methods

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Goldin (2010) presents a primary qualitative field and documentary case study of participatory water governance in the Breede-Overberg Water Management Area (Western Cape, South Africa) under the National Water Act (Act 36 of 1998) and Water Services Act (Act 108 of 1997). Drawing on contrasting local histories (Ruensveld/Duivenhoks commercial farming water schemes vs. the coloured fishing village of Kassiesbaai), primary interviews (2001-2004), and observations of Catchment Management Agency (CMA) public meetings and informal corridor ('stoep') spaces, the paper clearly articulates its aims (Q1: Yes), uses an appropriate qualitative approach (Q2: Yes), and states coherent thematic findings on how technocratic IWRM discourse, entrenched elite networks, and shame obstruct inclusive reform (Q9: Yes). However, appraised against the CASP Qualitative Checklist, the study exhibits high methodological concern (4 'Can't tell' and 2 'No' ratings across the 9 scored items): it contains no dedicated Methods section, leaving case/meeting selection rationale (Q3: Can't tell), participant recruitment (Q4: Can't tell), data collection procedures and sample size (Q5: Can't tell), and research ethics/consent (Q7: Can't tell) unreported, while omitting researcher reflexivity (Q6: No) and rigorous, transparent qualitative coding/analysis (Q8: No).
raw_response.overall_rating: High methodological concern (4 Can't tell and 2 No items out of 9 scored CASP criteria)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Primary qualitative field and documentary case study (stakeholder interviews, CMA public participation meeting and informal 'stoep' observations, and comparative local narratives in the Breede-Overberg Water Management Area, South Africa)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Aims and statutory context in Abstract and Sections 1.1-2 ([PDF Pages 1-3 of 18], pp. 195-197); comparative Breede-Overberg narratives (Ruensveld/Duivenhoks and Kassiesbaai) with primary interviews and secondary history in Section 4 ([PDF Pages 4-8 of 18], pp. 198-202); CMA meeting observations, 'stoep' ethnography, and interviews with officials, consultants, small-scale farmers, and councillors in Sections 6-7 ([PDF Pages 9-15 of 18], pp. 203-209) and Footnote 17 ([PDF Pages 15-16 of 18], pp. 209-210); synthesis in Section 8 ([PDF Page 16 of 18], p. 210). No standalone Methods section is present.
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The paper reports primary qualitative empirical fieldwork—specifically dated interviews with local councillors, a small-scale farmer, a water board respondent, and a WMA consultant (2001-2004), direct observations of DWAF/CMA public participation meetings and informal 'stoep' interactions, and comparative documentary/field narratives in the Breede-Overberg WMA (supplemented by 2003-2004 fieldwork noted in Footnote 17)—with no quantitative analysis or systematic review protocol. It therefore fits the CASP Qualitative Checklist for primary qualitative field/documentary case studies.
